hook.text: Organic food costs 30–100% more than conventional. Consumers pay for values, not just nutrients.

buildup.text: Higher costs come from lower yields, more labor, expensive certification, and smaller-scale processing.

discovery.text: The premium lets organic farmers earn comparable income despite lower production volumes.

twist.text: If conventional farming paid for its environmental damage—pollution, soil loss—the price gap would shrink or reverse.

climax.text: Organic food sales have grown 10–15% annually for two decades. Consumers are voting with their wallets.

punchline.text: Conventional food is cheap because nature absorbs the hidden costs.

quiz.question: Why might the organic price premium shrink if environmental costs were included?
options: Conventional prices would rise to reflect hidden environmental damage

details.summary: The organic premium is the higher price consumers pay for certified organic food compared to conventional equivalents. This topic examines the size of the premium, what drives it, and whether it covers the true costs facing organic farmers.
details.whyItMatters: The organic premium funds the higher labor costs, lower yields, and certification expenses that organic farmers face. Understanding this premium is central to evaluating whether organic farming is viable at scale.
takeaways: Organic food typically costs 20-100% more than conventional equivalents
The premium reflects higher labor costs, lower yields, and certification expenses
Not all of the retail premium reaches farmers due to supply chain markups

faq.question: Why does organic food cost more than conventional food?
faq.answer: Organic farming has higher labor costs (manual weed and pest management), lower yields (typically 10-25% less), expensive certification processes, and smaller production scale. These increased costs are passed on as a price premium to consumers.

faq.question: Do organic farmers actually earn more despite higher costs?
faq.answer: Studies show organic farmers often earn comparable or higher net profits than conventional farmers because the price premium usually exceeds the higher production costs. However, profitability varies significantly by crop, region, and market access.
